title: Continents and Crustal Features
seo_title: Grade 8 Science: Continents and Crustal Features Worksheets (MATATAG)
standard_code: Grade 8, Quarter 3: Earth and Space Science
standard_text: The distribution of continents and oceans; the Earth's layers; evidence for moving plates; crustal features (mountains, trenches, volcanoes) formed where plates interact. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 8, Quarter 3: Earth and Space Science)
meta_desc: Free Grade 8 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 3: Earth and Space Science): earth's layers, evidence for plate tectonics, plate boundaries, plates in motion and earthquakes and hazards. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Earth's crust is broken into moving plates.
key_sub: Plates move a few centimeters a year.
body_html:
How to think about it

The Earth has a crust, mantle, outer core and inner core. The crust and upper mantle are broken into plates that move on the hotter mantle below. Convection currents in the mantle move the plates a few centimeters each year, and the continents have moved over millions of years.

At plate boundaries plates move apart (divergent), collide (convergent) or slide past each other (transform). This makes earthquakes, volcanoes, mountains and deep trenches. The Philippines lies between the Philippine Sea Plate and the Eurasian Plate, so it has trenches such as the Philippine Trench, many volcanoes and frequent earthquakes.

Example

Which layer of Earth do we live on?

The thinnest, outer layer

Answer: the crust

Example

What happens at a convergent boundary?

Plates move toward each other.

Answer: plates collide

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the plates float on liquid magma all the way through.
  • Thinking plates move fast enough to see.
  • Mixing up the crust and the core.

items.q: Jose reads: “A long underwater mountain chain runs down the middle of the Atlantic Ocean.” What is the best explanation?

Wind blew the fossils across the ocean.

items.q: Which evidence best supports this idea: “Antarctica was once near the equator.”

Magnetic stripes on the seafloor are symmetric on both sides of the ridge.
Coal from tropical swamps is found in Antarctica.
items.e: Match the evidence.

items.q: Rafael studies the Alpine Fault in New Zealand, where plates slide past each other. What kind of plate boundary is it?
items.e: At a transform boundary, plates slide past each other.

items.q: Rafael studies the Andes Mountains, where plates push together. What kind of plate boundary is it?
items.e: At a convergent boundary, plates push together.

items.q: About how fast do plates move?
c: a few centimeters per year, about as fast as fingernails grow
items.e: Slow, but it adds up over millions of years.

items.q: Rodel studies the Himalayas, where plates push together. What kind of plate boundary is it?
items.e: At a convergent boundary, plates push together.

items.q: Nico studies the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. What happens to the plates there?
c: The plates slide past each other.
items.e: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is at a divergent boundary.

items.q: Nico studies the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where plates move apart. What kind of plate boundary is it?
items.e: At a divergent boundary, plates move apart.

items.q: Rodel studies the volcanoes of Japan. What happens to the plates there?
c: The plates slide past each other.
items.e: The volcanoes of Japan is at a convergent boundary.

items.q: Who first proposed continental drift using fossils and continent shapes?
items.e: He proposed it in 1912.

items.q: Do continents float on the ocean?
c: No. Continents are part of plates that move over the hot, slowly flowing mantle.
items.e: The mantle rock can flow very slowly.

items.q: Why couldn't Mesosaurus have swum across the Atlantic?
c: It was a small freshwater reptile that could not cross a salty ocean.
items.e: Its fossils support the idea that the continents were joined.

items.q: What was Pangaea?
c: a supercontinent that existed about 300–200 million years ago
items.e: It broke apart into today's continents.

items.q: What often happens where an ocean plate meets a continental plate?
c: The ocean plate sinks, forming a trench and volcanoes.
items.e: The denser plate sinks.

items.q: What are tectonic plates?
c: large pieces of Earth's outer layer (lithosphere) that slowly move
items.e: Continents and ocean floors ride on plates.

items.q: Nicole studies the East African Rift, where plates move apart. What kind of plate boundary is it?
items.e: At a divergent boundary, plates move apart.

items.q: Ana studies the volcanoes of Japan, where plates push together. What kind of plate boundary is it?
items.e: At a convergent boundary, plates push together.

items.q: Dennis studies Iceland splitting slowly, where plates move apart. What kind of plate boundary is it?
items.e: At a divergent boundary, plates move apart.

items.q: Angel studies the Alpine Fault in New Zealand. What happens to the plates there?

items.e: The Alpine Fault in New Zealand is at a transform boundary.

items.q: Which kind of plate boundary forms mid-ocean ridges?
c: no boundary: it is far from any plate edge
items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: A tsunami travels across the deep ocean at about 800 km/h. Joshua's town is 3,200 km from the earthquake. About how many hours does the town have to evacuate?
items.e: time = distance ÷ speed = 3,200 ÷ 800 = 4 hours.
